THE BOOKSTALL GIRL.
SWEET SMILES ALLIED WITH
SMARTNESS.
The bookstore girl is a new institution, but she is already to be found at several railway stations.

For instance, she is installed at the Westminster Bridge-road Station of the "Bakerloo" tube, and yesterday she was selling magazines and evening papers with a mingled dexterity and charm never possessed by a mere male clerk. The bookstore girl at Westminster Bridge-road is a young brunette with a pleasant manner, who with all her pleasantness never allows personal considerations to interfere with business. She stood in the midst of her stall yesterday afternoon, with a pencil behind her ear, the picture of keenness.
"I like the work," she said, "and find no difficulty in it. I get here at eight in the morning. Of course, before that I have had my two boys outside with the morning papers.

"Have I had any incidents in my work? No. I am busy in the morning checking the daily papers that have come in and dealing with the boys' money. Besides, I sell a good many papers myself from the stall here. All the customers are very nice to me. So are the railway officials. I have had the greatest kindness from everyone. In any kind of emergency I should ring up the manager at Waterloo.
"‘Evening News, sir?’ She turned briskly to a customer, folded a paper, handed it to him, took his halfpenny, and smiled sweetly.

While she went on with her work the customer on his way to the lift made a whispered confession in response to a question. "Whenever I come this way," he said, "I buy a paper whether I want it or not. I like to see the way she sells it."

Alderman Farrell, who will be installed as Lord Mayor of Dublin next week, selling papers in his shop. Mr. Farrell, who is seen with his wife, will have the honour of receiving the King and Queen when they visit Ireland.—(Daily Mirror photograph.)

NE.S ITEM-Lee Woo the great Hong Kong baseball writer has been engaged by a San Francisco paper to report the dilt games of the professional leagues in the West Lee hails from Pa in China. He became an adept in the art of playing shuttlecock at the age of ten and at 14 he was a chapion. Because of his superiority at the game he was ruled off and then had to contend himself with being umpire. At 16 when he was considered the greatest authority on the game he met a missionary that taught him baseball. A la American. He manufactured a set of gloves, balls, and bats and induced his followers to play the games. With Lee as umpire the game prospered until he was convinced for giving "bum depisions". He has now come to America and is conducting the column entitled "Stlike Outs". He is here seen watching a close play through a telescope after which he yells "Take out pitches man, him alm go by-by": 4/26/19.
